title: Why Don't Woodpeckers Get Headaches at 20 Hits/Sec? 🐦
description:
Woodpeckers hammer trees up to 20 times a second, so why don't they get concussions? High-speed video from a 2022 study shows a woodpecker's head isn't a shock absorber at all: it's a stiff hammer, and its tiny brain is what keeps it safe.

Sources:
https://www.sci.news/biology/woodpecker-pecking-11004.html
https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/woodpecker-skulls-dont-absorb-shock-like-previously-thought-180980426/
https://www.scienceabc.com/nature/animals/how-woodpeckers-dont-get-concussions.html

Animated in the Kawaii Anime style.

script: Woodpecker pecks would concuss you. They do up to 20 a second, around 12,000 a day, and never get a headache. Why? For years, people said their skull was a shock absorber, like a built-in helmet. But in 2022, scientists filmed woodpeckers with high-speed cameras. And the head didn't cushion anything. The beak and the brain stopped together, like one stiff hammer. Which honestly makes sense. Nobody builds a hammer with a sponge inside. It would waste every swing. So the real secret is size. A woodpecker's brain is hundreds of times smaller than yours, and tiny brains can take much bigger jolts. That jolt that would knock you out? For them, it's well below the danger line. They'd have to hit twice as fast to get hurt. So if a woodpecker were as big as you, could it still peck?
key_facts: Woodpeckers can peck up to about 20 times a second and around 12,000 times a day
A 2022 Current Biology study (Van Wassenbergh et al.) filmed black, pileated and great spotted woodpeckers with high-speed cameras
The head does not absorb shock: beak and brain decelerate together, so the head acts as a stiff hammer
Each peck's deceleration exceeds the concussion threshold for humans, but small brains tolerate far bigger decelerations
Normal pecking stays well below a woodpecker's concussion threshold; they would need to hit about twice as fast to be at risk
